cards.title: A. K. Manocha and Sanjaya Das
cards.sub: 19 January 2016 · CMD of IRCTC and MD of CRIS, joint press conference
cards.prompt: Indian Railways called a joint press conference in January 2016 over Tatkal. Name the IRCTC and CRIS chiefs who fronted it, the public claim they were there to rebut, and the evidence they published against it.
cards.body: Dr A. K. Manocha (CMD, IRCTC) and Sanjaya Das (MD, CRIS) answered sellers claiming their software books Tatkal in 10 to 20 seconds. Evidence: day-by-day tables of first-minute bookings, 25 December 2015 to 10 January 2016. The IRCTC column reads 0 for every 10:00:00-to-10:00:35 window; human counters booked about 2,000.
cards.answer: Dr A. K. Manocha, CMD of IRCTC, and Sanjaya Das, MD of CRIS. They rebutted the claim that scripting software books Tatkal tickets in 10-20 seconds, by publishing per-day tables showing zero IRCTC Tatkal bookings in the first 35 seconds of the opening window.

cards.title: Money debited but ticket not booked
cards.sub: IRCTC customer advisory · undated page, PDF print header 17 April 2018
cards.prompt: IRCTC keeps a standing advisory for one failure rather than one outage. What is the failure called, where does IRCTC place the blame, and how long is the passenger's money gone before it returns?
cards.body: The advisory blames "any failure or delay" across the customer, bank and gateway chain, not the seat logic. Row one: "Payment Settled but Ticket Not Booked". IRCTC credits the amount back to the bank "on next day"; the bank credits the passenger "within 2-3 working days". A compensation, because you cannot roll a bank back.
cards.answer: "Money debited but ticket not booked", blamed on failure or delay anywhere in the customer/bank/payment-gateway/IRCTC chain. IRCTC returns the amount to the bank the next day and the bank credits the passenger within 2-3 working days — a compensating refund, not a rollback.

cards.title: irctcClockSync
cards.sub: 8 August 2016 · Kavish Dahekar · commit c9227b0129fb · 2.8 KB of Python
cards.prompt: A small 2016 GitHub project exists only because Tatkal opens on a fixed clock edge. What does it set, which HTTP field does it read to learn the server's time, what correction does it apply for network delay, and what accuracy does it claim?
cards.body: It requests IRCTC's login page, parses the Date response header for the server's time, then adds rtt/2 plus its own parsing time before setting your system clock. The README: bookings "start sharply at 10:00AM and 11:00AM IST", and the script syncs "as close as ±1 second".
cards.answer: It sets your system clock from the Date response header of IRCTC's login page, adding back half the measured round-trip time, and claims ±1 second accuracy — so the claim can be fired at the instant the quota opens.

cards.title: Rationing the contenders
cards.sub: Announced 11 June 2025 · in force 1 and 15 July 2025 · Ministry of Railways
cards.prompt: Booking capacity had gone up more than sevenfold by 2015 and the Tatkal race still did not settle. What did the Ministry of Railways change in July 2025 instead of tuning the system further, and what does that move say about where the contention actually lived?
cards.body: From 1 July 2025 only Aadhaar-authenticated users may book Tatkal online; from 15 July, Aadhaar OTP is mandatory. The same announcement bars authorised agents from the opening 30 minutes — 10:00 to 10:30 for AC, 11:00 to 11:30 for non-AC. The fix moved out of the lock and into the door.
cards.answer: Aadhaar authentication for online Tatkal from 1 July 2025, Aadhaar-based OTP from 15 July, and agents shut out of the first 30 minutes. The contention was over who was allowed to contend, so the answer was admission control, not a better hold.
